text.content: By this point, the Vela Systems canvas has a defined memory architecture: boundaries between shared and private state, write ownership per key, a recovery path after interruptions, and four log positions that produce a trace across the full execution chain. The architecture is sound on paper. What it has not been tested against is the specific ways memory and state tend to fail in production — not because the architecture was wrong in design, but because edge cases in real usage expose gaps that controlled testing does not surface.

text.content: The Vela team is preparing to hand the system to thirty users. Before that happens, they need to work through a set of scenarios that represent the realistic failure surface of a multi-agent system like theirs: cases where memory causes an agent to return irrelevant or stale output, cases where state causes incorrect routing or silent duplication, and cases where the combination of the two causes a failure that neither individually would produce. Your job in this lesson is to work through those scenarios on the Vela canvas and design a safeguard for each one.

text.content: Summary

rich_text.plain_text: Summary

text.content: Anticipating failure modes before integration is the difference between a system that works in a controlled test and one that holds up under real usage. The five scenarios in this lesson represent the categories of memory and state failure that appear in production multi-agent systems: stale memory caused by reset timing, state contamination within a session, unsafe persistence to a shared store, concurrent-session key collision, and recovery paths that restore to an incorrect or stale state.
